name: Iris Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I study international business with Spanish. A normal week is two lectures on markets and trade, three Spanish classes that start at eight, and a team case study where I'm the one who builds the spreadsheets. I use AI every day: to quiz me on vocabulary, to draft emails to my teachers, and to check my models. On Thursday evenings I sing in the church choir, and Sunday afternoons I tutor two schoolkids in maths.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how does money work for you right now, between family, the part-time job and the course?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My parents run a hardware shop in a small town, Holm, and they pay for my room in a student flat, which is about half my costs. Tutoring brings in 60 a week and I put 20 of that into an index fund, because a teacher told me to start early. I'm careful, but I like having numbers that grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here is the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, it's a handy tool and it keeps me ahead in class. I'd tell the choir that the world isn't ending, and our sopranos can stop worrying. Online I'd probably post a short note about how I use it to learn Spanish, because I'm proud of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calm. I'd still have my degree, my tutoring and the fund. If the tools don't change much, my advantage is that I already know how to use them and most people don't. The only worry is whether my parents' shop can keep up with the big chain that opened last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on: study, tutor, invest. I'd add a third pupil and put 25 into the fund. I'd apply for an exchange year in Spain, because the language is a real edge in international business. And I'd help my parents set up an online page for the shop, which they've been putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a comfortable version, where steady work pays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra time the small gains give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop, definitely. The chain across the ring road sells the same screws cheaper, and Dad's margins have dropped. It's not an AI problem, it's a normal-world problem, but it's the thing I think about on the train home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still invest and tutor the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, even more. A fund is a slow, quiet way of building something, and tutoring teaches me to explain things. If nothing dramatic happens, patient people win.

say: I'd tell the choir the world isn't ending and our sopranos can stop **worrying**.
I'd post a note on how I use AI to learn **Spanish**.
think: I already know how to use the tools, which is my **advantage**.
My parents' **shop** is under pressure from the big chain across the ring road.
do: Add a third **pupil** and put 25 a week into the fund.
Apply for an **exchange year** in Spain and help set up the shop's online page.
feel: **Calm**, because steady work pays off in this version.
S0.quote: The chain across the ring road sells the same screws cheaper, and Dad's margins have dropped.
fieldNote: Her calm comes from her **habits**, and the one worry is her parents' shop.
She treats Spanish and the fund as slow, patient edges.
She plans to help the shop get online, which parents have put off.

steps.text: Take a third maths pupil for Sunday tutoring
Put 25 a week into the index fund
Set up an online page for my parents' hardware shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift and we should lean into it. I'd tell friends to learn the tools and to learn how to explain things, because that's the part people still pay for. I'd say we need fair rules, but not rules that stop people starting things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of entry-level business roles get squeezed, like analyst, assistant and junior marketing. I use AI to do what an intern does, and it's already decent. But I think people who can sell, lead and speak Spanish with a customer will still be needed, so I'm trying to be that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up the skills that go with the tools: sales, negotiation and Spanish. I'd try for a summer internship at a small export firm, where I'd do real work. I'd add tutoring pupils, invest 30 a week, and try making a simple website to offer maths and Spanish lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. The job market will be tighter, and I can feel that, but I think I'm in a decent spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does daily use shape what you think is coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents. Dad's shop sells to builders who may need fewer people and fewer materials if projects get cheaper, but it's more that online sellers get better at pricing, and Dad's margins are thin. I'd help them learn to use the tools for ordering and ads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A friend from the choir, Marta, who's studying graphic design. Her course is full of people who say the tools are cheating. I'd worry she's going to be left behind because she refuses to try them, and I'd say so to her gently.

say: I'd tell friends to learn the tools and learn to **explain** things, since that's what people still pay for.
I'd say we need fair rules but not rules that stop people **starting things**.
think: Entry-level business roles like analyst and **junior marketing** get squeezed.
People who can sell, lead and speak **Spanish** with a customer will still be needed.
do: Aim for a summer **internship** at a small export firm.
Invest **30 a week** and build a simple website for maths and Spanish lessons.
feel: **Uneasy**, but not scared, because I feel I'm in a decent spot.
S1.quote: I use AI to do what an intern does, and it's already decent.
fieldNote: She knows from daily use that the tools already do **intern work**.
Her plan is to be the person who can sell, lead and speak Spanish.
She worries about a choir friend, Marta, who refuses to try the tools.

steps.text: Apply for a summer internship at a small export firm
Launch a site offering maths and Spanish tutoring
Invest 30 a week in the index fund
Show my parents how to use AI for the shop's ads

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge, and I'd say it plainly: I'm worried, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. I'd also say people should keep working, keep helping each other and keep their families close. In church I'd say hold on to what you can control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree might be worth far less by 2029. If AI does almost any thinking work, then a business and languages graduate with no experience is competing with something free. I'd feel scared and also annoyed that I'd done everything right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work as fast as I can: more tutoring pupils, more money into the fund, and every internship I can find. I'd learn how to build small tools with AI, so I'm someone who can run the machines. And I'd talk to my parents about their savings and how long the shop can last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My head says it's a plan, and my stomach says it's not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years do to your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the shop is hands-on, so it will last longer than most jobs, because robots come a few years after. But I'd say the ordering, the accounts and the advertising will change fast. I'd suggest they keep strong customer relationships, because a local shop is trusted in a way a website isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about the hardware shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd stop planning for a career and plan for an income. I'd take any honest work that pays and keeps a roof over my head, and I'd keep investing, because it's the one thing that grows on its own.

say: I'd say I'm worried and not going to **pretend** otherwise.
In church I'd say hold on to what you can **control**.
think: My degree might be worth far less by **2029**, competing with something free.
I'd feel scared and annoyed that I did everything **right**.
do: Take more tutoring **pupils**, put more into the fund and seek every internship.
Talk to my parents about their **savings** and how long the shop can last.
feel: **Anxious**: my head says it's a plan and my stomach says it isn't enough.
S2.quote: With two years I'd stop planning for a career and plan for an income.
fieldNote: Her plan shifts from career to **income**, which is the sharpest change across her answers.
She advises her parents that a local shop is trusted in a way a website isn't.
She remains an investor, because it's the one thing that grows on its own.

steps.text: Take four more tutoring pupils over the next two terms
Raise my fund contribution to 40 a week
Learn to build small AI tools for local firms
Sit down with my parents to plan the shop's savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have enough time to adapt if we're smart. I'd say people should build skills and savings, and stay out of debt, and that government should keep rules light so new firms can start. I'd put it on a post and talk about it at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel pretty good. I'd graduate in 2029, with a year in Spain behind me, and a couple of work years before the big change. I'd be able to build a small business by then, and the fund would be a decent size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, take the exchange year, and pick up two internships. I'd start a small tutoring and translation service and use AI to run most of it. I'd keep investing 40 a week and aim to have a first real business running by graduation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of tension. It's a manageable version if I keep my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what would you do that you couldn't do in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope they move the shop online now, in a small way, and teach a part-time employee to run it. Then when the big change comes they have a shop that works even if Dad retires. I'd offer to build the first version over summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope your parents do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm racing, with five I'm building. Building is better, because the things you make in five years are worth more than the things you scramble to make in two.

say: I'd say we have enough time to adapt if we're smart and keep **debt** low.
I'd say government should keep rules light so new **firms** can start.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with a year in Spain and a couple of **work years** left.
The fund would be a **decent size** by then.
do: Finish the degree, take the **exchange year** and do two internships.
Start a tutoring and **translation** service run mostly with AI.
feel: **Calm**, with a bit of tension, as long as I keep my head.
S3.quote: With two years I'm racing, with five I'm building.
fieldNote: Five years turns her from **racing** to building, in her own words.
She wants her parents to move the shop online now, in a small way.
Her optimism rests on savings, language skills and low debt.

steps.text: Take the exchange year in Spain and do two internships
Start a tutoring and translation service run with AI
Invest 40 a week and avoid all debt beyond fees
Build the first version of the shop's online store over summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to be bold. A decade is enough to build something, and I'd tell friends to start businesses, learn the tools, and keep their families strong. I'd say it will be a better world if people take responsibility and don't wait to be rescued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm quite excited. I'd be 28, with several years of experience and maybe a small company of my own. The thinking part of business would be mostly done by AI, and the human part, trust, deals, leadership, would be mine. I'd also like to be someone who can help my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, work two years at an export firm to learn, then start my own company, probably using AI for most of the back-office. I'd keep investing, and aim for a house deposit by 27. I'd help my parents turn the shop into a small online and local business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited. I can see how this could be good for me and for my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years: what do you picture yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them work and faith and family will matter more, not less. Machines do the thinking, but a person who shows up, keeps a promise and takes care of others still matters. That's what a choir does too. It's a group of people who show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the choir about faith and work in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's easy to be scared of the future, and it's also easy to be careless. I'd like us to be the ones who prepare and look after others while we do.

say: I'd tell friends to start **businesses** and keep their families strong.
I'd say it will be a better world if people take **responsibility** and don't wait to be rescued.
think: The thinking part of business would be mostly AI, and the **human part** would be mine.
I'd like to be someone who can **help** my parents.
do: Finish the degree, work two years at an **export firm**, then start my own company.
Invest steadily for a **house deposit** by 27 and help the shop go online.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, because I can see it being good for my family.
S4.quote: Machines do the thinking, but a person who shows up, keeps a promise and takes care of others still matters.
fieldNote: Her **faith and family** view is that human trust becomes more valuable once machines think.
She sees herself starting a company, with AI doing the back office.
She ends on responsibility: prepare, and look after others.

steps.text: Finish the degree and work two years at an export firm
Start my own company with AI running the back office
Invest steadily toward a house deposit by 27
Turn the family shop into a local and online business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I can handle most things if I've got a plan and time, and two years takes both. What would help is clear rules that let people work, start businesses and keep what they earn, plus training that employers actually respect, not just certificates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I think this is a good thing in the end. I do, if people are free to use it. I use it to learn faster, and I think work and faith and family will matter more, not less. But I'd say that to my parents and they'd be worried about the shop.

headlineQuote: Work and faith and family will matter more, not less.
portrait: Iris is 18 and studies **international business with Spanish**, sings in the church choir and tutors two schoolkids in maths.
She uses AI every day, invests 20 a week in an **index fund** and is curious and comfortable with risk.
She is traditional and favours free markets, work and family, and wants **fair rules**, not handouts.
Her mood is calm or uneasy in most worlds and anxious only in the **two-year** one, where she has no time.
She moves first: she learns, earns and invests, then helps her parents' **hardware shop** adapt.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, because two years removes both her plan and the time to carry it out.
whatWouldHelp: She wants clear **rules** that let people work and start businesses, plus training employers actually respect.
